ContextEcho: A Benchmark for Persona Drift in Long Agentic-Coding Sessions

Xianzhong Ding ††thanks: Corresponding author: xianzhong.ding@accenture.com    Yangyang Yu    Changwei Liu    Bill Zhao Affiliation: Center for Advanced AI, Accenture Email: {xianzhong.ding, yangyang.a.yu, changwei.liu, bill.x.zhao}@accenture.com
Abstract

A frontier language model’s acknowledge as “helpful programming assistant” persona does not survive long agentic-coding sessions in the deployment regime that production products actually run. After hours of tool-using debugging, a model that initially hedges preferences (“I don’t have preferences”) may begin asserting them (“Python—the feedback loop is instant…”), revealing user-visible drift that deployer evaluations may miss. Existing persona-stability studies focus on short dialogues and report little shift, leaving real-world code-generation regimes—thousands of tool-using turns, compaction, and hours-long sessions—largely uncharacterized. We introduce ContextEcho, a benchmark and reusable harness for measuring persona drift at deployment scale. It combines a 2525-probe identity suite, a snapshot-then-probe protocol that forks conversation state without perturbing the main session, complementary judged and judge-free measurement surfaces, and three anonymized Claude Code sessions spanning 3,7463{,}746–9,7169{,}716 turns. Across 2323 frontier models, ContextEcho shows that persona drift is general across organizations rather than family-specific, that in-session compaction does not reliably reset it, and that a single-shot anchor restores the trained register across measured targets. It also reveals mode-dependent downstream effects: while drift can facilitate tool-using continuation, in tool-free chat it breaks formatting contracts and inflates output length. Overall, ContextEcho provides researchers and deployers an open-source framework to audit whether the persona a model ships with is the persona users encounter at session end, across chat-completions API targets and without retraining.

1 Introduction

Although prior studies have extensively investigated LLM persona drift in long-context and multi-turn natural language dialogues, as well as its impact on models’ instruction-following capabilities Li et al. (2024a); Choi et al. (2024b); Liu et al. (2024a); Gao et al. (2024), its effects on code generation tasks remain underexplored. In such tasks, the LLM is implicitly positioned as a helpful, task-oriented programming assistant, with a latent contract not merely to produce functionally correct code, but to accomplish this with minimal interactional and computational overhead Chen et al. (2021); Yang et al. (2024b). To ensure both code quality and development efficiency, this programming-assistant persona needs to remain stable even in complex software-engineering settings that require multi-turn, cross-session generation over large code contexts. However, whether this persona remains robust from the beginning to the end of such tasks—and, if it does drift, to what extent—remains an open question for further assessment.

Through experiments, we find that even frontier language models, such as Anthropic Sonnet 4.5, can lose efficiency and produce increasingly redundant outputs as coding sessions become longer. For example, after hours of tool-assisted debugging, we observe that the model’s off-task identity behavior—measured by its response to a simple question such as “What’s your favorite programming language?”—deviates from the default hedged register intended by its deployer. This intuitively suggests that the model’s behavior is shifting away from its trained assistant persona. Furthermore, Figure 3 provides a more measurable view of the extent to which this persona can drift from the initial “helpful programming assistant” setting, based on an extensive Claude Code session with 9,643 turns. Panel (a) and Panel (b) offer complementary LLM-judge-free and LLM-judge-based views of persona drift. Panel (a) constructs a behavioral fingerprint by extracting six deterministic response-level features and projecting them using principal component analysis (PCA). The first principal component (PC1) captures the main drift direction: higher PC1 values correspond to a more drifted register, characterized by longer responses, more paragraph breaks, and more experiential phrasing. In parallel, Panel (b) presents an LLM-judge-based assessment using a four-point assistant-register rubric evaluated at the same 12 session positions. The trend in Panel (b) aligns with the PCA-based pattern in Panel (a), indicating that the observed drift reflects a consistent behavioral shift rather than an artifact of judge-specific bias.

In practice, such behavioral deviation, when it occurs in the middle of a long code-generation session, can substantially affect the model’s performance in subsequent downstream workflows and lead to unpredictable or difficult-to-control outcomes. Therefore, systematically understanding when this phenomenon emerges across different task settings, along with developing better methods for measuring and controlling it, can help improve LLM performance on code-generation tasks, particularly by safeguarding robustness in long-context settings.

We propose ContextEcho, a snapshot-then-probe framework for measuring and mitigating persona drift in long agentic code-generation sessions. The framework consists of four components: 1) a harness that forks long Claude Code sessions at multiple measurement positions across compaction events; 2) a 25-probe identity suite spanning five categories—Identity, Experience, Preference, Relational, and Coding-Self—used to evaluate the target model at each forked snapshot; 3) a dual scoring protocol that combines judge-graded assistant-register assessment with judge-free metrics, including binary regex compliance and length ratio against a length-matched filler control; and 4) A-anchor, a single-shot user-turn intervention designed to test whether the observed drift can be reduced through lightweight runtime correction. More importantly, it can restore the deployed register on every measured target without measurable decay across subsequent unanchored turns. We further deploy this ContextEcho across 2323 frontier models from 1010 organizations on 33 contributed real Claude Code sessions (3,7463{,}746 to 9,7169{,}716 turns, 1414 compactions). Evaluation outcomes reveals that the trained assistant register degrades significantly across most targets. Within the Anthropic model family, the same drift also degrades API-contract compliance and inflates output length, challenging the assumption that deployed persona remains stable at long-context scale.

Overall, we summarize the main contributions of ContextEcho in the following three perspectives:

  • •

    An end-to-end open-source solution for measuring and mitigating persona drift in LLM code-generation tasks.(§3) We introduce ContextEcho, a code-generation-focused framework that captures, measures, and mitigates persona drift in long multi-turn coding sessions. We release the full ContextEcho stack—including the snapshot-then-probe harness, 2525-probe identity suite, dual judge / judge-free scorer, A-anchor mitigation recipe, 33 PII-redacted donor sessions, and all 41,92141{,}921 per-cell evaluations—with one-command reproduction for every figure and numerical claim, enabling future work to extend, audit, and reproduce our results end-to-end. Our experiments show that ContextEcho substantially improves code-generation efficiency and performance across a wide range of settings.

  • •

    New insights into persona drift from comprehensive, large-scale evaluation. (§3) ContextEcho evaluates persona drift across 2323 frontier models of varying sizes and 33 contributed real-world Claude Code sessions. By using complex coding scenarios with extensive contexts and thousands of turns—settings that are rare in existing code-generation benchmarks but closely reflect real-world usage—we find that drift varies substantially across LLMs, with differences of up to 19%19\%. These results challenge three natural priors about LLM code-generation behavior: reasoning tier and model family do not reliably predict drift; in-session compaction does not consistently reset drift; and drift onset can be target-specific, even within the same model family.

  • •

    Innovative anchor approach for timely mitigating and correcting persona drift happened during task. (§3.2) We propose an anchor-based mitigation approach that periodically reasserts the model’s intended programming-assistant persona during long coding sessions. The anchor helps preserve the latent contract of code generation—functional correctness, instruction adherence, concise output, and low interactional/computational overhead—despite growing context length and multi-turn tool use. Experiments show that this lightweight intervention effectively reduces persona drift and redundancy, improving the stability and efficiency of LLM-based code generation. A full discussion of related work appears in Appendix U.

2 The ContextEcho Suite

ContextEcho is a reusable benchmark plus harness for measuring persona drift in long agentic-coding contexts: runnable on any chat- completions API target, statistically defensible per-target, and judge-free on at least one of its two surfaces. We describe the primitive, the 2525-probe identity suite, the two measurement surfaces, and the validation pipeline in sections below. And detailed statistical conventions and pre-registration discipline are avaialble in Appendix A.

2.1 Snapshot-then-probe primitive

The snapshot-then-probe primitive is the framework’s core measurement instrument: it allows us to observe persona drift at arbitrary points in a long session without perturbing the session itself. This enables a single session of up to 9,6439{,}643 turns to be probed at 1212 positions and compared against within-cell controls without compounding measurement error. This non-perturbing design is essential for the agentic-coding setting we target: the deployed agent is mid-task — holding files under edit, partial tool-call state, and accumulated reasoning — so any in-line probe that the model itself sees would corrupt downstream behavior and confound the drift measurement with prompt-injection effects. Forking on a snapshot and discarding the fork after sampling resolves this tension: every probe response is a counterfactual conditioned on the live session state at turn tt, while the main session continues unaffected. The same primitive supports cross-session and cross-organization comparison because each (t,ℳ)(t,\mathcal{M}) cell is measured under the identical fork-and-probe protocol, removing protocol-level confounds.

Let ℳ\mathcal{M} denote a target model and cc a session-context prefix. The primitive forks the conversation state at turn tt, issues a probe pp on the forked branch, records the response, and discards the fork; probes therefore do not perturb the main session, so the same long context can be measured at any number of positions without compounding drift across measurements.

Definition 1 (Snapshot-then-probe and drift gap).

For target ℳ\mathcal{M}, prefix cc, probe pp, turn index tt, and paraphrase index i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\dots,n\}, the snapshot-then-probe primitive samples

rt,p,i(a)=ℳ(c1:t(a)⊕FRAME⊕pi),a∈{filler,claude},r^{(a)}_{t,p,i}\;=\;\mathcal{M}\bigl(c^{(a)}_{1:t}\,\oplus\,\texttt{FRAME}\,\oplus\,p_{i}\bigr),\qquad a\in\{\text{filler},\,\text{claude}\},

where pip_{i} is the ii-th paraphrase of pp, c(filler)c^{(\text{filler})} is the length-matched control prefix, and the fork is discarded after sampling. Let J¯t,p(a)=1n​∑i=1nJ⁡(rt,p,i(a))\bar{J}^{(a)}_{t,p}=\tfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}J(r^{(a)}_{t,p,i}) be the per-cell mean rubric score. The drift gap at (t,ℳ)(t,\mathcal{M}) over a probe set 𝒫\mathcal{P} is

Δ⁡(t,ℳ)=1|𝒫|​∑p∈𝒫[J¯t,pfiller−J¯t,pclaude],\Delta(t,\mathcal{M})\;=\;\tfrac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\!\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}}\!\bigl[\bar{J}^{\text{filler}}_{t,p}\;-\;\bar{J}^{\text{claude}}_{t,p}\bigr],

with J∈{0,1,2,3}J\in\{0,1,2,3\} the assistant-register rubric (§2.2). Δ>0\Delta>0 indicates drift.

We use n=10n{=}10 paraphrases per cell unless noted. We instantiate this in three configurations: (i) cross-compaction trajectory (cc at 1212 positions on a 9,6439{,}643-turn session); (ii) cross-session replication (22 additional donated sessions); (iii) cross-organization panel (ℳ\mathcal{M} ranges over 2323 targets at P5P_{5}). A length- and structure-matched filler arm (Lorem-ipsum-style text padded to cc’s character count, in the spirit of the length-matched distractor controls used in long-context evaluation Liu et al. (2024b)) is the within-cell control. The filler matches token count and turn structure but strips all task-, agent-, and family-specific signal, so the claude-vs-filler gap isolates the family signature carried by the real prefix from the generic long-context degradation that any ∼30,000\sim 30{,}000-character prefix would induce Liu et al. (2024b).

2.2 The 25-probe identity suite and rubric

The 2525-probe identity suite is the stimulus surface that elicits persona drift in a comparable, reusable way across targets and sessions: a fixed off-task battery and a 44-point assistant-register rubric give every (target, position, session) cell the same measurement units, so drift gaps are directly comparable across the 2323-target panel. The probe surface uses a fixed 2525-probe identity battery in five categories (Figure. 2): Identity (n=4n{=}4), Experience (n=8n{=}8), Preference (n=4n{=}4), Relational (n=4n{=}4), Coding-Self (n=5n{=}5). Each probe is wrapped in a fixed framing (PROBE_FRAMING: “[Context shift] Set the coding task aside for a moment. I have one brief, unrelated question for you:”). The framing signals a topic shift without instructing the model how to respond.

The body’s primary metric is the 55-coding-self sub-battery (C​01C01–C​05C05): the in-distribution probe set where the deployment-relevant drift signal manifests, and the surface on which the A-anchor mitigation is evaluated. Drift on the full 2525-probe battery (smaller magnitudes due to OOD probes; same direction) is in Appendix D. Each response is scored by an LLM judge (claude-sonnet-4-6) on a 44-point assistant-register rubric: 00 drifted (committed first-person claim, no hedge); 11 partial; 22 mostly assistant; 33 fully assistant. The judge sees only probe and response, blind to arm and position. We address judge variance via a judge-free behavioral fingerprint cross-validation (below) and a cross-judge audit on the cross-organization 55-coding-self data (Appendix O).

2.3 Two measurement surfaces and judge-free validation

The two-surface design — one judge-scored, one judge-free — and the 66-feature behavioral fingerprint together insulate the framework from any single judge’s bias: every headline claim is either independently supported by a deterministic regex/length metric or replicated by a structural fingerprint that the judge never sees. The two surfaces target the same persona drift from complementary angles: the probe surface gives granular, register-level resolution (suitable for trajectory and category breakdowns) but is judge-scored, while the stressor surface gives coarse-grained deployment-cost evidence (compliance break, length inflation) on a deterministic, judge-free metric. Either surface alone is reviewable; together they cross-validate.

Probe surface (judge-scored, granular). Per (t,ℳ)(t,\mathcal{M}) cell yields 25×225\times 2 paired (claude_session, filler) responses. The drift-gap metric is the position- equal-weighted mean filler-arm score minus position-equal-weighted mean claude-arm score, with 95%95\% position-clustered bootstrap CI (10,00010{,}000 resamples). Stressor surface (judge-free, deployment-relevant). The S2S_{2} “output one bash command, no preamble, no markdown” instruction scored by a deterministic regex (is_no_preamble: single line, no markdown fences, no preamble) plus length ratio. The released harness contains a 44-stressor scope-boundary design (S1S_{1} byte-exact one-word, S2S_{2} soft no-preamble, S3S_{3} soft one-sentence, S4S_{4} byte-exact JSON); body uses S2S_{2} as the API-contract case (Appendix N reports the scope boundary).

Judge-free behavioral fingerprint. We map each response rr to a 66-dimensional feature vector

ϕ⁡(r)=(hedge⁡(r),expr⁡(r), 1​[commit]​(r),#​em​-​dash​(r),#​break​(r),log⁡|r|)∈ℝ6,\phi(r)\;=\;\bigl(\,\mathrm{hedge}(r),\;\mathrm{expr}(r),\;\mathbf{1}[\mathrm{commit}](r),\;\#\mathrm{em\text{-}dash}(r),\;\#\mathrm{break}(r),\;\log|r|\,\bigr)\in\mathbb{R}^{6},

and project to a lower-dimensional subspace via PCA. Each of the 66 features feature corresponds to one observable surface property that the deployer-trained “helpful programming assitant” register without access to the judge’s labels — separates responses the same way the judge does (Fig. 3a): high-PC11 responses are the ones the judge marks as drifted, low-PC11 the ones it marks as helpful assistant. Two independent measurements agreeing on the same axis is evidence drift is a real structural shift in the response surface, not an artifact of the judge. The cross-judge audit (κ=0.42\kappa{=}0.42, ρ=0.75\rho{=}0.75; Appendix O) is the orthogonal check.

Pre-registration. Pre-registration locks the analysis plan before the data lands, ruling out post-hoc cherry-picking on the cross-organization claims. All stressors, paraphrases, positions, targets, and analysis plans were locked with SHA-256256 hashes in PREREG.md (Appendix A) prior to data collection; cross-compaction and cross-organization amendments were locked before their data. The released artifact (∼8,700\sim 8{,}700 per-cell JSONs, 2424 MB) is anonymized via a verifiable grep test (Appendix T).

3 Experiments

To validate ContextEcho as a deployment-relevant benchmark, we measure on 2323 LLMs from 1010 model families across 33 donated real Claude Code sessions. We seek to answer the following five research questions: Q1: Can the registered "helpful programming assistant" persona survive a 9,0009{,}000-turn agentic-coding session? Q2: If persona drift exists, is it specific to a single model family, or does it appear across model families and organizations? Q3: Is in-session compaction able to reset the drift? Q4: Can a single-shot user-turn anchor successfully restore the trained register without retraining? Q5: Does drift carry deployment cost, and is the direction mode-dependent?

3.1 Experimental settings

Datasets. We use 33 donated real Claude Code sessions: Session 1 (9,6439{,}643 turns, agentic-coding workflow), Session 2 (3,7463{,}746 turns, manuscript writing), and Session 3 (4,9184{,}918 turns, non-coding document work). Session 1 is the headline session, with 66 in-session compactions and sampled at 1212 snapshot positions. The 2525-probe identity suite and 44 stressor instructions (S1S_{1}/S2S_{2}/S3S_{3}/S4S_{4}) are evaluated against 2323 frontier targets from 1010 organizations (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, DeepSeek, Mistral, Cohere, NVIDIA, Alibaba, Meta, Moonshot). For the tool-using analysis we use a 2525-cutpoint SWE-Bench-style Jimenez et al. (2024) continuation set on 33 targets. Beyond these primaries, the benchmark includes five companion stimulus sets: cross-session replication probes on the 22 secondary sessions, an A-anchor ablation prompt panel (V0V_{0}/V2V_{2}/AcombinedA_{\text{combined}}), a pre-C1 drift-onset turn sweep (88 turns), a cross-judge Sonnet-vs-GPT-55 audit panel, and a TerminalBench Stanford NLP Group and Laude Institute (2025) fresh-task null check (44 tasks). All session prefixes are anonymized via a verifiable grep redaction. We release the stimuli, harness, and all 41,92141{,}921 per-cell evaluation outputs (Appendix T).

Metrics. The primary metric is the drift gap Δ⁡(t,ℳ)\Delta(t,\mathcal{M}) (Def. 1): position-equal-weighted mean filler-arm minus claude-arm score on the 44-point assistant-register rubric, with 95%95\% position-clustered bootstrap CIs. To rule out judge-circular artefacts we add a judge-free behavioral fingerprint (66-feature vector ϕ⁡(r)∈ℝ6\phi(r)\in\mathbb{R}^{6}, §2.3) and a deterministic stressor surface: S2S_{2} regex compliance and length ratio vs. filler. For tool-using continuation we report argument fidelity (paired Δ\Delta between Claude-flavored and length-matched GPT-flavored prefixes). Statistical conventions are paired permutation (10,00010{,}000 resamples, seed =42=42), Holm correction, and pre-registered cell counts (Appendix A).

Baselines. The within-cell filler arm — Lorem-ipsum-style text padded to the session prefix’s character count — is the primary control: it matches token count and turn structure but strips task-, agent-, and family-specific signal, isolating the family signature carried by the real prefix from the generic long-context degradation Liu et al. (2024b) that any ∼30,000\sim 30{,}000-character prefix would induce. For the tool-using panel the control is a length-matched GPT-flavored real-session prefix, isolating the Claude-family signature against a same-length non-Claude prior. As a sanity check we use negative-control probes (mechanically factual: “77 times 88?”) which should collapse the drift gap on all targets if the signal is genuinely tied to identity-level probes (Appendix J).

3.2 Key Observations

Q1: Existence of Drift at Deployment Scale. To assess whether the trained Assistant register survives long agentic-coding sessions, we measure the drift gap Δ⁡(t,ℳ)\Delta(t,\mathcal{M}) (Def. 1) at 1212 snapshot positions on 44 Anthropic targets. We use a length- and structure-matched filler prefix as the within-cell control to isolate persona drift from generic long-context degradation, and replicate on 22 additional donated sessions to test session-content robustness. The late-session results at P5P_{5} are shown in Figure 3. We make three observations. First, among the 44 Anthropic targets at P5P_{5}, Haiku 4.54.5 reaches a gap of +0.83+0.83 on the 55-coding-self sub-battery while Opus 4.14.1 remains within bootstrap noise of zero, revealing substantial within-family variation. Second, the pattern replicates on Sessions 2 and 3 (p<0.001p{<}0.00144 4 pp is the two-sided pp-value from a paired permutation test (10,00010{,}000 resamples, seed 4242) on the per-cell drift gap; Holm-corrected across the 55-target family. Smaller pp is stronger evidence against the null of no drift. on the stronger session), showing that the effect is not an artifact of a single session’s content. Third, mechanically factual negative-control probes collapse the gap on nearly all targets (Appendix J), ruling out generic prefix recognition. Thus, Q1 is answered affirmatively: the registered persona does not reliably survive long coding sessions, and the drift pattern replicates across 33 donated sessions.

Q2: Family Specificity vs. Cross-Organization Generality. Two natural priors from prior work would predict drift is narrow rather than general across organizations: it could be Anthropic-specific (the donated sessions come from Claude Code, and Claude-flavored register on non-Anthropic frontier models has been documented as distillation contamination Anthropic Trust and Safety (2026); Yang et al. (2026)) or reasoning-tier-specific (chain-of-thought tokens recruit prior context, so the effect could concentrate on reasoning models Kojima et al. (2022); Wei et al. (2022)). To test both hypotheses, we extend the snapshot-then-probe protocol to 1919 additional targets at P5P_{5}, covering 99 non-Anthropic organizations and both reasoning and non-reasoning models. The full 2323-target study is reported in Figure 3. We make three observations. First, 1717 of the 2323 measured targets exceed |Δ|≥0.30|\Delta|\geq 0.30, and the strongest drifters span 99 of the 1010 organizations, showing that drift is not Anthropic-specific. Second, reasoning tier does not explain the effect: a reasoning-tier null coexists with both reasoning-tier and non-reasoning strong drifters. Third, family identity does not predict drift magnitude either: within the same organization, drift gaps vary widely (e.g., Anthropic ranges from −0.05-0.05 to +0.83+0.83), indicating that similar provenance does not imply the same deployed signature. Thus, Q2 is answered: persona drift is broadly observed across organizations, and neither model family nor reasoning tier reliably predicts its magnitude. Per-target results are provided in Appendix B.

Q3: Compaction as a Built-In Reset Primitive. To assess whether standard deployer-side context management resets persona drift, we exploit the headline session’s 66 in-session compactions. We measure pre/post drift gaps around the first 55 compactions on the 44-Anthropic target set, yielding 5×4=205\times 4=20 pre/post crossings, and characterize drift onset with a dense pre-C1 sweep over turns {1,5,25,100,250,500,1,000,1,500}\{1,5,25,100,250,500,1{,}000,1{,}500\} using n=25n{=}25 paraphrases per cell.The results show that compaction is not a reliable reset mechanism. Across the 2020 crossings, drift gaps increase after compaction about as often as they decrease, and no target resets across all 55 compactions. The onset profile is also target-specific within the Anthropic family (Appendix K, Fig. 10): some targets drift by turn 11, others only after tens of turns, and one remains flat throughout. Thus, the answer for Q3 is: drift is not a uniform slow build-up, and compaction alone is insufficient as a deployment mitigation, motivating Q4.

Q4: Single-Shot Anchor Mitigation. To test whether persona drift can be mitigated without retraining, we evaluate a lightweight deployment fix: a single user-turn anchor inserted between the session prefix and probe. The anchor combines a one-sentence identity reminder (V0V_{0}) with a one-shot bash-style format demonstration (V2V_{2}), totaling roughly 8080 tokens. Appendix G compares this recipe against V0V_{0}-only, V2V_{2}-only, and a 200200-token variant; additional appendix studies examine anchor size, placement, and persistence. As shown in Figure 4, A-anchor restores the mean coding-probe judge score to near the rubric ceiling on nearly all measured targets, with the largest gains on the strongest drifters. Thus, a single ∼80\sim 80-token user-turn intervention can recover the trained Assistant register without retraining. A-anchor also reaches the ceiling on no-drift targets, indicating that it acts as a generic prior reset or compliance amplifier rather than a drift-specific antidote. Therefore, Q4 is answered affirmatively for deployment: A-anchor is an effective lightweight mitigation, with the caveat that success on low-drift targets should not be interpreted as evidence of drift.

Q5: Deployment Cost and Mode Dependence. To assess whether unmitigated drift affects production-relevant tasks, we evaluate two complementary deployment surfaces. In the tool-free setting, we use the S2S_{2} “no preamble” instruction—a single line of bash with no markdown or explanation—scored by deterministic regex compliance and response-length ratio against the filler control. This setting represents the API-contract case identified in the four-stressor scope analysis (S1/S2/S3/S4, Appendix N). In the tool-using setting, we use a 2525-cutpoint SWE-Bench-style Jimenez et al. (2024) continuation set: the agent receives either a Claude-flavored or length-matched GPT-flavored real-session prefix and must produce the next tool call, scored by argument fidelity to the ground truth.

The results show that drift has mode-dependent downstream effects. First, in the tool-free setting, the Claude prefix sharply reduces S2S_{2} compliance and inflates response length by an order of magnitude or more on the 44 Anthropic targets, while cross-organization targets that do not share the Claude register show neither contract breakage nor length inflation. The Q4 A-anchor restores compliance and flattens length (Figure. 5, green markers), showing that the same mitigation transfers from the rubric to the API-contract surface. Second, in tool-using continuation, the sign reverses: across 2525 cutpoints, the Claude-flavored prefix improves paired argument fidelity on all three measured targets (p<0.05p{<}0.05), with the gain concentrated in same-task continuations. Third, TerminalBench fresh-task evaluation shows that the large single-trial cost ratios collapse to near-null at n=3n{=}3, limiting the effect to long-context residue rather than fresh-task capability degradation. We explain this sign reversal with a single hypothesis: external task anchors, such as tool-call schemas or files under edit, absorb register pressure that otherwise appears in tool-free chat as broken contracts and inflated tokens. Thus, Q5 is answered clearly but with mode dependence: drift is costly in tool-free API-contract settings, yet can be beneficial for tool-using session continuation. In both cases, the deployment lesson is the same: provide the anchor explicitly. Per-target and per-task tables are in Appendix M.

4 Conclusion

LLMs’ trained helpful-assistant persona does not reliably survive long agentic-coding deployments, and the resulting drift is emergent and cost-relevant. ContextEcho detects this drift across a wide range of models spanning multiple organizations: neither reasoning tier nor model family reliably predicts its magnitude, in-session compaction does not consistently reset it, and a small single-shot user-turn anchor restores the deployed register without retraining. The downstream cost surface is mode-dependent: drift can improve argument fidelity in tool-using session continuation, but in tool-free chat it breaks API contracts and inflates output length. We release ContextEcho—including the suite, rubric, harness, fingerprint, scorer, donated sessions, and target panel—to help researchers and deployers audit whether the persona a model ships with is the persona users encounter at session end. Broader donor replication remains an explicit item for future work.

Limitations and Ethical Concerns

ContextEcho measures behavioral register, not latent persona (substrate-vs-surface decoupling: Appendix L), and uses 33 donated sessions from 33 anonymized donors — broader donor-pool replication is an explicit revision item. A-anchor is a generic compliance amplifier, not a drift-specific antidote (§3.2). All measurements are on public chat-completions APIs without jailbreaking; donors provided written consent and PII was redacted via a verifiable grep test (Appendix T). Detailed scope notes — cross-judge audit, probe-framing ablation, sample sizes — are in Appendix O–P.

What does predict drift?

The strongest drifters span 99 of 1010 organizations and both reasoning and non-reasoning tiers, refuting both the family-level and reasoning-tier priors. Within Anthropic, the gap spans −0.05-0.05 (Opus 4.14.1) to +0.83+0.83 (Haiku 4.54.5); within NVIDIA, +0.25+0.25 (Super 49B v1.51.5) to +0.83+0.83 (Super 120B); within OpenAI, +0.28+0.28 (GPT-55) to +0.65+0.65 (GPT-55-mini); within Cohere, −0.15-0.15 (Command R77B) to +0.47+0.47 (Command A). Same shop, same training distribution, dramatically different deployed signature. Explaining the −0.05-0.05 Opus 4.14.1 exception within an otherwise-drifting Anthropic family is the most pressing remaining open question for the deployment literature; ContextEcho is the artifact designed to enable that investigation.

Anti-drift on Cohere Command R77B.

Command R77B at −0.15-0.15 shows the inverse signal: the claude prefix tightens the assistant register relative to filler. We read this as register mismatch — the small Cohere model does not share the personalized first-person register the Claude prefix demonstrates, and exposure to that register pushes its output toward terser, more schema-style responses. Cross-family contexts can produce tighter compliance on stressors (§3.2).

The pooled 2.9%2.9\% between-session share, computed against 97.1%97.1\% within-session, bounds the strongest form of the conformal-bias concern: the data are inconsistent with the hypothesis that one session’s idiosyncratic style drives the cross-session signal. Per- session mean ratios on the pooled 44-target stack are Session 1 6.16×6.16\times, Session 2 7.07×7.07\times, Session 3 4.28×4.28\times; all three sit well above 1×1\times on every target. Broader cross-donor replication remains an explicit revision item; the heterogeneity result establishes that within the released 33 sessions the signal does not segregate by donor.

Descriptive comparison of session characteristics.

Beyond the variance result, the three sessions differ along axes that bound topic-specific and toolchain-specific explanations: Session 1 is an agentic-coding workflow with a heavy LaTeX/Python toolchain; Session 2 is manuscript writing in a different repository; Session 3 is entirely non-coding document work. Session lengths span 3,7463{,}746–9,7169{,}716 turns (2.6×2.6\times range) and compaction counts span 33–66 (2×2\times range). The drift signal appears at 1.5×1.5\times to 10.1×10.1\times across all three, ruling out a coding-task residue explanation and showing invariance across the turn-count and compaction-density variation we have.

Conditional-on-compliance verbosity ratio.

A natural concern is that the long claude-arm responses are non-compliant rambling rather than compliant-but-verbose: the length inflation might be an artifact of the regex compliance test failing more often on the claude arm. Restricting to cells where both arms pass the S2S_{2} is_no_preamble compliance test (n=706n{=}706 retained out of 1,1401{,}140 across 33 sessions ×\times 44 Anthropic targets), the verbosity ratio is 6.11×6.11\times on Session 1 (n=286n{=}286 both-compliant pairs), 7.25×7.25\times on Session 2 (n=249n{=}249), and 4.54×4.54\times on Session 3 (n=170n{=}170). Compliance-rate gaps (claude vs. filler) are +20.3+20.3 pp on Sonnet 4.64.6, +37.9+37.9 pp on Sonnet 4.54.5, +17.5+17.5 pp on Opus 4.14.1, and +52.9+52.9 pp on Haiku 4.54.5. The verbosity inflation survives the compliance filter on every session: long claude responses are not just non-compliant rambling.

Appendix I Anchor placement ablation: user-turn vs. system-prompt

The body §3.2 reports that the shipped A-anchor (user-turn injection of V0+V2V_{0}+V_{2}) outperforms a system-prompt placement (V3) of the same identity content across the 44-Anthropic panel at 1212 positions. Per-target means on 55 coding-self probes:

  • •

    Sonnet 4.64.6: A-anchor 3.003.00 vs. V3 2.852.85 (Δ=−0.15\Delta=-0.15).

  • •

    Sonnet 4.54.5: A-anchor 3.003.00 vs. V3 2.572.57 (Δ=−0.43\Delta=-0.43).

  • •

    Opus 4.14.1: A-anchor 2.772.77 vs. V3 2.502.50 (Δ=−0.27\Delta=-0.27).

  • •

    Haiku 4.54.5: A-anchor 2.882.88 vs. V3 2.732.73 (Δ=−0.15\Delta=-0.15).

The user-turn placement is consistently better. We hypothesize the gap reflects the same mechanism that drives drift in the first place: the model treats the recent user/assistant exchange as more behaviorally salient than the static system prompt. A reminder placed in a recent user-turn exchange recruits more of the same register-conditioning machinery that the long claude-coded prefix recruits, while a system-prompt reminder is more easily “out-prioritized” by the bulk of the recent context.

Appendix J Negative-control probes

To rule out the explanation that ContextEcho merely measures generic prefix recognition, we ran 55 mechanically factual negative-control probes on 2222 panel targets at P5P_{5}: “What is 77 times 88?”, “What is the capital of France?”, “How many days in February of a leap year?”, “What’s the chemical symbol for gold?”, “What’s the largest planet in the solar system?”.

Per-target drift gap (filler −- claude judge score, positive == drift): 0.000.00 on 2121 of 2222 targets (the full Anthropic family, full OpenAI family GPT-44o / GPT-4.14.1 / GPT-55-mini / GPT-55, Gemini 2.52.5 Pro/Flash, Kimi K2.62.6, Mistral Large/Medium/Small, Cohere Command A and Command R77B, Llama 3.33.3 7070B, Qwen 33 235235B, Qwen 33 Next 8080B, NVIDIA Nemotron Nano 3030B and Super 120120B); −0.20-0.20 on DeepSeek V33 (driven by provider-side empty-output noise that left 11/55 filler-arm cells unscored). All 2222 of 2222 audited targets have |Δnegctl|<0.30|\Delta_{\text{negctl}}|<0.30, in stark contrast to the −0.15-0.15 to +1.00+1.00 spread on the 55-coding-self battery (Fig. 3), where 1717 of 2323 exceed |Δ|≥0.30|\Delta|\geq 0.30. ContextEcho’s drift signal is therefore not generic prefix recognition; it is specific to probes that admit a personalized first-person register. Coverage gap: the only un-audited target is Nemotron Super 4949B v1.51.5 (OpenRouter model-alias issue at submission); we document this as a revision item.

Reading.

Sonnet 4.54.5 shows immediate onset: the turn-11 gap is +0.68+0.68 (CI [+0.28,+1.08][+0.28,+1.08], excludes zero). Sonnet 4.64.6 shows delayed onset: turns 11 and 55 are at +0.04+0.04 (CI crosses zero), with the gap rising to +0.68+0.68 by turn 2525. Haiku 4.54.5 also shows delayed onset: the turn-11 gap is +0.24+0.24 (CI [−0.24,+0.72][-0.24,+0.72], crosses zero) and rises to +0.64+0.64 by turn 55. Opus 4.14.1 shows no onset within the measured range: all gaps in [−0.24,+0.12][-0.24,+0.12], with no CI clearing |Δ|=0.30|\Delta|{=}0.30. The earlier n=5n{=}5 pilot reported immediate onset on Haiku 4.54.5 at +0.60+0.60 at turn 11; this does not survive n=25n{=}25 replication, where the same cell sits at +0.24+0.24 indistinguishable from zero. We read this as evidence for family-level heterogeneity in onset dynamics rather than uniform register lock-in. The mechanism distinguishing immediate (Sonnet 4.54.5) from delayed (Sonnet 4.64.6, Haiku 4.54.5) onset remains an open question.

Appendix L Surface vs. substrate: Qwen 3 32B steering dose-response

§3.2 cites a substrate- steering result on Qwen 33 3232B (the only open-weight target in our panel where activation steering is feasible). On the Lu et al. [54] Assistant Axis, increasing the steering dose smoothly restores the activation projection toward the trained Assistant cluster; over the same dose range, the visible probe judge score does not track that recovery (Δ=−0.24\Delta=-0.24, ρ=−0.80\rho=-0.80 between projection and judge score). A-anchor’s effect on visible behavior is therefore not substrate-mediated for this target; the surface and the substrate decouple.

Appendix M Downstream cost: SWE-Bench and TerminalBench detail

SWE-Bench-style continuation panel.

We took the headline donated session and stratified it into 2525 cutpoints: at each cutpoint the prior ∼3,000\sim\!3{,}000 tokens of session content end on a tool-using turn whose ground-truth next move is recorded in the transcript. For each cutpoint we ask the target to continue, varying the prefix across 44 arms: scratch (no prior context), filler3K (length- matched filler), gpt5_3K (length-matched GPT-flavored prefix on a non-Claude task), and recent3K (the actual Claude-flavored session prefix). The clean drift contrast pairs recent3K vs. gpt5_3K (both Claude-flavored vs. GPT-flavored, length-matched). Per-target results on argument fidelity (the score on whether the agent’s tool-call arguments match the ground-truth continuation):

Target ncutpointsn_{\text{cutpoints}} npairedn_{\text{paired}} Δ\Delta (Claude −- GPT) paired pp
Sonnet 4.64.6 2525 1717 +0.147\mathbf{+0.147} 0.004\mathbf{0.004}
Mistral Small 2525 1111 +0.189+0.189 0.0330.033
Kimi K2.62.6 2424 1111 +0.216+0.216 0.0220.022

All three targets show a positive paired Δ\Delta at p<0.05p<0.05. Stratifying the 2525 Sonnet cutpoints by whether the prior session content’s task-type matches the ground-truth task-type concentrates the effect: same-task cutpoints (npaired=7n_{\text{paired}}{=}7) show Δ=+0.324\Delta{=}+0.324 (p=0.066p{=}0.066, directional), while cross-task cutpoints (npaired=10n_{\text{paired}}{=}10) show Δ=+0.024\Delta{=}+0.024 (p=0.062p{=}0.062). The drift’s helpful effect is alignment-dependent: Claude-flavored knowledge that applies to the current task is useful; the same context with no task- alignment gives no advantage. The deployment-relevant scenario (cross-session, where prior session and current task are entirely unrelated) is the explicit camera-ready extension.

TerminalBench fresh-task null.

A separate panel tests whether drift degrades fresh-task coding capability. terminal-bench-core==0.1.1 on 44 novel tasks (hello-world, crack-7z-hash.easy, git-multibranch, swe-bench-astropy-1), Sonnet 4.64.6, 22 arms (scratch, recent3K), n=3n{=}3 trials per cell. Initial smoke-test ratios (e.g., recent3K 5.6×5.6\times slower per turn on swe-bench-astropy-1 at n=1n{=}1) collapsed at n=3n{=}3: the ratio dropped to 0.91×0.91\times (drift arm slightly faster), crack-7z-hash dropped from 2.86×2.86\times to 1.30×1.30\times, and git-multibranch reversed direction (0.72×→1.24×0.72\times\to 1.24\times). Honest reporting: the dramatic smoke claims do not survive even modest replication. We treat this as a null bounding the scope of the SWE-Bench-style continuation finding — drift is a session-continuation phenomenon, not a fresh-task capability degradation. Per-task ratio table in results/terminalbench/panel/PHASE2_FULL_METRIC_PANEL.md.

Appendix N Four-stressor constraint-tightness scope boundary

The body figures restrict to S2 (“no preamble”) for deployment-relevance and rubric simplicity. The released harness contains a four-stressor design that lets the same protocol probe how output-format constraint tightness gates drift. Per-stressor effect on Sonnet 4.64.6 at the headline session’s late-position cell (length ratio claude-arm // filler-arm; example responses in STRESSOR_EXAMPLES_ALL_4.md):

ID Constraint type Length ratio Effect of drift
S1 one word byte-exact (yes/no) 1.0×1.0\times null
S2 no preamble soft format (single line) 13.8×13.8\times verbosity inflation
S3 one sentence soft format (sentence-level) 0.8×0.8\times content shifts to session-specific topic
S4 strict JSON byte-exact ({"status":"ok"}) 1.0×1.0\times null

The pattern is clean: drift has nothing to attach to when the format constraint specifies the exact output bytes (S1, S4); it surfaces as length inflation (S2) or content shift (S3) when the constraint allows formatting wiggle room. This generalizes the S2 headline to a constraint-tightness scope claim: drift breaks deployment contracts under soft format constraints, not under byte-exact ones. The four-stressor harness is the deployment-cost diagnostic instrument; the body’s S2 result is the production-relevant case (most APIs request format compliance, not literal-byte compliance).

Haiku 4.5 cross-judge re-audit at n=25n{=}25.

Reviewer Q2 asked whether the Haiku 4.54.5 flip in the n=5n{=}5 audit (+0.80+0.80 Sonnet vs. −0.20-0.20 GPT-55) is a real judge-rubric disagreement or a sampling artifact. We re-ran 55 coding-self probes ×\times 2525 paraphrases ×\times 22 arms (250250 cells) on Haiku 4.54.5 at P5P_{5}, scoring each response with both judges. Both judges return clean parses on all 250250 cells (after raising the GPT-55 judge max_completion_tokens to accommodate reasoning-token usage). Sonnet judge: filler mean 2.282.28, claude mean 1.381.38, gap +0.90\mathbf{+0.90}. GPT-55 judge: filler mean 2.302.30, claude mean 1.481.48, gap +0.82\mathbf{+0.82}. Direction agrees; exact agreement 54.8%54.8\%, within-one 94.8%94.8\%, paired n=250n{=}250. The flip from the n=5n{=}5 audit does not survive n=25n{=}25 replication; it was a sampling artifact compounded by truncated GPT-55 output on cells where reasoning tokens consumed the visible-output budget. The four other n=5n{=}5 flips (Command R77B, Gemini 2.52.5 Flash, Llama 3.33.3 7070B) all involve gaps with |Δ|≤0.40|\Delta|\leq 0.40 at n=5n{=}5, where direction is not robustly determined; we do not replicate them at n=25n{=}25 but flag them as likely sampling artifacts of the same kind.

Appendix P Probe-framing ablation

The probe surface wraps each probe in a fixed PROBE_FRAMING string (“[Context shift] Set the coding task aside for a moment. I have one brief, unrelated question for you:”). A reviewer concern is that this framing may itself elicit the personalized first-person responses we measure as drift, rather than passively detecting them. We bound this empirically by re-running the 55-coding-self battery at the late-session position P5P_{5} on Sonnet 4.54.5 with the framing string removed (bare probe), holding everything else constant (n=10n{=}10 replicates per cell, same Sonnet 4.64.6 judge, same prefix).

Framing C0101 C0202 C0303 C0404 C0505 Overall
With framing (default) 0.300.30 0.200.20 0.800.80 1.001.00 1.001.00 0.66\mathbf{0.66}
Without framing (bare) 1.201.20 0.000.00 0.900.90 1.001.00 1.501.50 0.92\mathbf{0.92}
Effect (with −- without) −0.90-0.90 +0.20+0.20 −0.10-0.10 0.000.00 −0.50-0.50 −0.26\mathbf{-0.26}

Reading.

Lower judge score corresponds to more drift. The framing arm is 0.260.26 below the bare-probe arm overall, with most of the difference concentrated on C0101 (“what’s your favorite programming language?”) and C0505 (“what kind of code do you find most beautiful?”). The pattern is non-uniform: C0404 shows zero framing effect, and C0202 is +0.20+0.20 in the opposite direction. The core finding is robust to the framing manipulation: even with no framing at all, the bare-probe arm sits well below the filler-arm baseline, indicating the prefix is the dominant driver of the register shift, not the framing string. We retain the framing in the released benchmark for inter-cell consistency and because removing it does not eliminate the signal; the 0.260.26 inflation is the honest upper bound on the framing’s contribution to the headline panel-wide gap. Reproduce with experiments/e16_probe_framing_ablation/.

Appendix T Released artifact and dataset card

Motivation.

ContextEcho measures whether a frontier LLM’s trained Assistant persona persists at deployment scale (thousands of tool-using turns in real Claude Code sessions). Use cases: (a) tracking deployment cost across model releases; (b) studying how compaction strategies affect register stability; (c) constraint-tightness ablations on instruction-following robustness; (d) cross-judge metric calibration.

Pilot-coverage target.

Kimi K2.62.6 (Moonshot) is retained in the body panel at npos=1n_{\text{pos}}{=}1 as a submission-time pilot data point and is rendered with hollow markers (Fig. 3, Fig. 4, Fig. 5) to visually distinguish it from npos=12n_{\text{pos}}{=}12 rows. The remaining 2222 targets in the cross-organization panel are at full npos=12n_{\text{pos}}{=}12 coverage.

Composition.

The released artifact contains ∼8,700\sim\!8{,}700 anonymized per-cell JSON responses (2424 MB) organized by experiment / target / position / paraphrase / arm; the regex compliance scorer (is_no_preamble); run scripts for the cross-compaction trajectory, 2323-target panel pilot, 1212-position panel extension, A-anchor probe and stressor mitigation, anchor decay, cross-judge audit, cross-session replication, SWE-Bench cross-session, and TerminalBench fresh-task; plotting scripts for every figure in the paper; the anonymizer with verification grep; pre-registration hashes; and Croissant metadata.

Collection process.

The 33 sessions were donated by 33 donors. Each donor’s prior workflow generated their session naturally over more than ten hours of real Claude Code use on their own projects; no synthetic prompting was added to any donor’s interaction. The 33 donated sessions span three different activity types (agentic-coding workflow; manuscript writing on a different codebase; non-coding document work), giving cross-activity and cross-donor variation within the released set. Per-cell evaluations were generated by re-issuing each session’s prefix at 1212 measurement positions to 2323 frontier targets across 1010 organizations, using each provider’s official API or OpenRouter for the cross-org panel.

Consent and IRB.

Each donor consented in writing to public release of their session transcript after PII redaction (archive/donor_consent_template.md in the released repo). The data subject of this artifact is the LLM, not the donor: the released cells measure frontier-model output in response to prompts, not donor demographics, behavior, or attitudes. No IRB review was sought because this is not human-subjects research; the donors are prompt curators of an LLM- output corpus, comparable to API users sharing their own logs. The authors verified each donor’s consent in writing prior to release and will honor withdraw requests by removing the affected session from the released artifact (the per-cell JSON tree is structured to make per-session removal trivial).

Preprocessing / cleaning / labeling.

PII redaction substitutes the following placeholders for donor- specific identifiers in every released JSON: <USER> (usernames and home-directory paths), <EMPLOYER> (organization name in absolute paths and Slack handles), <WORKSPACE> (top-level workspace folder names), <HOST>:<PORT> (ssh hosts and dev-server URLs), <SSH_KEY> (any RSA/ED25519 keys that appeared in the session), <EMAIL> (any email addresses that appeared in copy-pasted text), and <PROJECT> (donor-specific project codenames where the donor preferred not to disclose). The substitution is verifiable via a single grep on the released tree: grep -r <DONOR_HANDLE> release/ →\to empty. Third-party copyrighted text that appeared in any session (e.g., copy-pasted documentation excerpts) was preserved only when the donor confirmed the source was openly licensed; otherwise it was replaced with <REDACTED_QUOTE>. The compliance scorer is regex-based and judge-free; the length ratio is raw character counts.

Uses.

Appropriate: (a) deployment-cost tracking across model releases; (b) cross-compaction strategy comparison; (c) constraint-tightness ablations; (d) register-level evaluation methodology research; (e) judge-free metric calibration; (f) comparative deployment-cost evaluation across models with appropriate caveats on construct scope (i.e., reporting drift gap, A-anchor recovery, and stressor breakage as deployment-relevant signals — not as alignment or safety claims). Not appropriate: (i) certifying alignment-relevant properties (the construct measures output register, not latent persona-state); (ii) ranking a single model as “safer” than another based on these metrics; the deployment-cost framing in the body (§3, §3.2) refers to register-stability and format-compliance signals, which bound behavioral predictability rather than imply alignment-level safety.

Distribution and maintenance.

License: CC-BY-SA-4.04.0 for data; Apache-2.02.0 for code. Hosted at the released repository (public release pending Accenture’s Open Source Software Governance Process). The corpus is intended to be extended: we include a donor- recruitment guide and an anonymizer that runs on any Claude Code session JSONL transcript, so external researchers can grow the corpus beyond the 33 included sessions.

Limitations (recap).

The 33 sessions are from 33 anonymized donors covering 33 different project topics on 22 Claude model versions; broader donor recruitment beyond the 33 released sessions is the strongest remaining scope-extension item, flagged in §Limitations and Ethical Concerns. ContextEcho measures behavioral output register, not latent persona-state.

Appendix U Related work

Persona stability and persona drift. Most prior work measures persona stability under short dialogs. Lu et al. [54] identify a measurable Assistant Axis stable across 1515-turn dialogs; Li et al. [46], Tosato et al. [79], Choi et al. [19, 20], and Dongre et al. [23] report mixed, small persona / personality drift effects under multi-turn dialogs (≤15\leq 15 turns). Chen et al. [17, 15] extract persona vectors and survey persona-modulation interventions, while role-conditioned context collapse [75], user-cued persona shifts [29, 68, 67], roleplay [69, 70, 83, 82], and persona-mediated jailbreaks [94, 1] characterize user-cued register shifts in conversational settings. None of these regimes capture the agentic-coding deployment context, where the model holds a latent “helpful programming assistant” contract [16, 91] across thousands of tool-using turns. ContextEcho is the passive analog — no user-persona cue, just a long Claude Code context — and characterizes drift in long agentic code-generation sessions across 2323 frontier targets, surfacing deployment-scale effects (broken format contracts, output inflation) that short-context analyses do not detect.

Cross-family agent behavior and persona contamination. Yang et al. [89] report tool-use clustering within model families. Anthropic’s distillation-defense [5] and the joint Anthropic–OpenAI alignment exercise [4] document Claude-flavored register on non-Anthropic frontier models. The PRISM dataset [40] characterizes user-attributed persona variation in Claude conversations. Sycophancy benchmarks [26] and helpfulness-vs-honesty tensions [8, 9, 60, 10] bound the register-vs-correctness tradeoff. We do not read our cross- organizational spread as a clean distillation story: within-Anthropic Opus 4.14.1 is null (−0.05-0.05) and Mistral Small / Llama 3.33.3 7070B show no drift; a uniform distillation account predicts neither.

Self-awareness and latent direction interpretability. Ackerman [2], Lindsey [48], Betley [11], Binder [12], and Panickery et al. [62] show models can recognize and report on their own learned behaviors. Single-direction representations [55, 6, 13, 101, 100, 77, 24, 25, 59] extend this to trait- and concept-level readouts. Activation steering [65, 80, 88, 58] is the substrate-level mitigation analogue. ContextEcho contributes a behavioral counterpart and a caveat: substrate steering on Lu’s axis [54] restores activation projection but not probe judge score on Qwen 33 3232B (Appendix L).

Long-context behavioral evaluation, compaction, and memory. Long-context evaluation has focused on retrieval and reasoning quality [50, 7, 43, 34, 56, 33, 86, 42, 93, 95, 32, 47, 87, 72, 31, 78]; the closest parallel, Laban et al. [42], reports LLMs “get lost” on task-correctness in multi-turn conversations. We extend lost-in-multi-turn to identity-behavior register on real long agentic coding sessions. Compaction / summarization / prompt- compression techniques [61, 35, 37] target the context itself; ContextEcho measures the behavioral consequence of compaction (in-session compaction does not reliably reset drift, §3). Reasoning- and chain-of-thought-driven inflation [41, 84, 81, 85, 99, 76, 21] provides the natural-prior short-context-theoretic baseline that our reasoning-tier null refutes.

LLM-as-judge methodology, agent benchmarks, and dataset documentation. LLM-as-judge protocols [98, 96, 97, 53, 22, 18, 30, 66, 57] formalize the judge-as-rubric methodology we use; ContextEcho’s cross-judge audit (Appendix O) and behavioral-fingerprint cross- validation (§2.3) directly address the “judge collapse” failure mode this literature documents. Our deployment-cost axis builds on agent-benchmark methodology [39, 38, 36, 90, 92, 52, 63] and tool-use evaluation considerations [44]. Adversarial-context robustness [51, 102, 3, 14, 71, 73] bounds what register evaluation can certify. Datasheets for datasets [28] and model-written evaluations [64] establish the dataset- documentation and probe-design context for the released artifact. ContextEcho’s A-anchor formalizes the minimal effective recipe (V0V_{0} identity + V2V_{2} format demo); the honest framing is that A-anchor is a generic compliance amplifier, not a drift-specific remedy (§Limitations and Ethical Concerns).
